Problems Without an OS
A - Concurrency & Scheduling
Multiple activities need CPU at different rates:
• Sensor sampling (50 ms)
• Communication (500 ms bursts)
• UI refresh (100 ms)
• Logging (every 60 s, but blocking)
Concurrency needs preemptive scheduling →
an OS responsibility.
|--read(5ms)--|--process(5ms)--|--display(3ms)--|--COMM BLOCK(200ms)--|
→ missed 50 ms sampling ticks
Why this fails on baremetal:
• Serialized loop cannot respect independent
cadencaes
• Blocking operations delay everything
• Interrupts help responsiveness but not preemptive,
priority-based scheduling
Problems Without an OS
B - Memory Protection & Isolation
Baremetal has:
• No process isolation
• No protection domains
• No crash containment
Result: one bug can corrupt the whole system (invalid pointer, buffer overflow).
Isolation requires MMU + OS process model
(or MPU in small RTOS contexts).
With MMU (Linux) or MPU (some RTOS) can constrain damage:
• a fault kills one process or triggers a protection fault instead of corrupting unrelated code.
• MPU protects regions
• MMU provides full process isolation.
Problems Without an OS
C - IPC & Composition
• Features must talk reliably: sensor → control → comms → storage.
Without OS:
• Adhoc queues, globals, flags → Fragile, nonportable, non-observable
With an OS:
• standard IPC (queues, pipes, shared memory, sockets) makes flows explicit, testable,
loggable.
• Standard mechanisms: pipes, message
queues, shared memory, sockets
• Easier to test, log, and maintain
• Isolation reduces blast radius; IPC makes
interactions explicit & testable.
Problems Without an OS
D - Filesystems & Persistence
Real products need:
• Logging to flash
• Configuration storage
• Durable updates
E - Networking Stack
• TCP/IP, TLS, DHCP, DNS—these are huge.
• Baremetal approaches: Limited stacks, difficult integration, fragile edge cases
F - Observability & Debugging
• Baremetal debugging is often limited.
• VFS (Virtual Filesystem)
• Standard semantics
• Buffering and caching
Linux provides:
• Mature network stacks
• Tools and libraries
• Sockets abstraction
• Logs (kernel/user)
• Process state (/proc)
• Trace tools (strace, perf)
• Profiling and metrics

Choose the right tool based on complexity + constraints + risk.
When to Choose BareMetal
Characteristics:
• Hard real-time with microsecond-level deadlines
• Ultralow power, ultralow footprint
• Simple feature set; deterministic control loops
• No memory protection; single image; fast boot (milliseconds)
Baremetal excels when you know exactly what must happen,
when, and forever, and the device has one job. You sacrifice
isolation and rich features to get predictability and speed.
BareMetal: Use Cases
Motor Control / BLDC Commutation
Pacemaker / Implantable Medical Controller
• Deadline: PWM update and current sensing in tens
of microseconds
•
Determinism: Strict ISR timing
•
Why baremetal: Minimal latency paths; tight
control loop in ISR; resource-constrained MCU
•
Deadline: Beat detection and pulse timing in
milliseconds
•
Determinism: Safety-critical, simple control logic
•
Why baremetal: Highly constrained hardware;
validated single-purpose behavior; rigorous
certification
Capacitive Touch /
LowPower Sensors
Keyless Entry FOB /
LowDuty RF
•
Deadline: Scan cycles in hundreds of
microseconds
•
Why baremetal: Simple, event-driven, ultra-low
energy
•
Deadline: RF timing windows in milliseconds
•
Minimal feature set; fast wake → action → sleep
When to Choose an RTOS
Characteristics:
• Hard/firm real-time tasks with bounded latency
• Deterministic scheduling with priorities (SCHED-like internal policy)
• Typically, no MMU → limited memory isolation
• Moderate complexity; timer services; queues; semaphores
• Small footprint; faster boot than Linux
• Common pitfalls: priority inversion (fix with priority inheritance), timer drift (use monotonic
clocks), ISR-only work (move to deferred tasks)
RTOS gives structure—tasks, priorities, timers—without
full OS isolation or giant subsystems. Think deterministic
control with moderate complexity.
RTOS: Use Cases
Quadcopter Flight Controller
Industrial Servo / CNC Axis Controller
•
Deadlines: Sensor fusion loop (IMU/Gyro) 1–
2 kHz,
control outputs <1 ms jitter
•
Why RTOS: Tasks for sensor read, attitude
estimation, control output; priority-driven
preemption; still lightweight
•
Deadlines: Motion control <1 ms jitter
•
Why RTOS: Deterministic scheduling + timers;
modest networking via lightweight stacks; simpler
than Linux, more structured than baremetal
Automotive ECU
– Airbag Control
Smart Metering /
LowTier Gateways
•
Deadlines: Sensing/actuation <1–5 ms
•
Why RTOS: Deterministic tasks, AUTOSARstyle
scheduling, watchdog integration; no need for
Linux’s full user space
•
Requirements: Meter readout tasks + modest
comms (PLC/ZigBee) + small file logging
•
Why RTOS: Balances real-
time needs with modest
I/O complexity; footprint constrained
When to Choose Embedded Linux
Characteristics:
• Feature rich: filesystems, networking, security, drivers, update systems
• Process isolation (MMU): one crash ≠ total device failure
• Soft real-time is typical; hard real-time possible with PREEMPT_RT, CPU isolation, mlockall, and tuned
I/O
• Larger footprint; boot time generally longer (can be optimized)
• Excellent observability and maintenance story
Embedded Linux shines when you need many moving parts: networking,
storage, UI, updates, security. If you also need realtime, you can combine
Linux (for features) with RT tuning or pair it with an MCU/RTOS for the tightest
loops.
Embedded Linux: Use Cases
Automotive Infotainment (IVI) / Digital Cluster
Industrial Gateway / Edge Compute
•
Tasks: UI rendering, multimedia, navigation,
connectivity, OTA updates
•
Real-time: Soft real-time for UI responsiveness; some
hard real-time delegated to dedicated MCUs (e.g.,
speedometer from CAN on separate controller)
•
Why Linux: Complex feature set + isolation + security +
vendor driver support
•
Tasks: Protocol conversion (Modbus/OPC-UA), secure
telemetry (MQTT/TLS), local analytics, fieldbus interfaces
•
Real-time: Requires bounded latencies for field I/O;
PREEMPT_RT + CPU affinity can deliver submillisecond
jitter
•
Why Linux: Networking, storage, containers, remote
management; rich tooling
Home/Enterprise Router
Autonomous Mobile Robots
•
Tasks: NAT, firewall, WiFi, DHCP/DNS, VPN, captive
portal, logging
•
Real-time: Mostly soft real-time; high throughput over
deterministic hard deadlines
•
Why Linux: Mature network stack, drivers, security
patches, extensibility
•
Tasks: SLAM, path planning, sensor fusion, vision
pipelines, safety zones
•
Real-time: Some control loops offloaded to
microcontrollers; Linux runs complex perception and
planning with tuned real-time threads
•
Why Linux: Libraries (OpenCV, ROS2), IPC, logging,
updates, security, driver availability
